'Bespoke' mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows (https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/oct/23/mrna-vaccine-melanoma-cancer-breakthrough-australia)
【turn1116news18】 [wordlim: 100] Published: today; A groundbreaking phase III clinical trial has shown that a personalised mRNA vaccine, intismeran, significantly reduces the risk of melanoma recurrence or death. Customised to target up to 34 gene mutations specific to an individual's cancer, intismeran was tested alongside the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab in 1,137 high-risk patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed. After two years, 82% of patients receiving both treatments were alive and recurrence-free, compared to 70% treated with pembrolizumab alone, marking a 42% lower risk of cancer recurrence or death. The trial, conducted across 157 global sites and led from Australia, is the first to demonstrate positive phase III results for an individualised cancer vaccine. Experts hail it as a transformative development in oncology, enhancing the immune system’s ability to recognise and eliminate melanoma. However, the treatment is not universally effective, and long-term benefits remain under investigation. Regulatory approval and further studies are required before wide-scale availability, potentially taking several years.
‘Bespoke’ mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows
Date: Fri Oct 23 04:27:18 2026 UTC

A personalised mRNA-based melanoma vaccine significantly reduces the risk of cancer recurrence or death within two years, new clinical trial results show.
The vaccine, intismeran, is custom-made to target genetic mutations unique to an individual's melanoma. It is the first individualised cancer vaccine to show positive results in a phase III clinical trial.
The Australian-led trial included 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but were at high risk of it returning.
All were treated with an immunotherapy drug called pembrolizumab for twelve months, and some were also given the personalised intismeran vaccine.
The trial found that at two years post treatment, the combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% compared with treatment with pembrolizumab alone.
 Related: It costs $230 out-of-pocket to see a dermatologist. Many Australians go without - despite soaring skin cancer rates  
Prof Georgina Long, medical director at the Melanoma Institute Australia and 2024 Australian of the Year, described the findings as "a foundational shift in our approach to cancer", allowing scientists to "harness ... the immune system in a more personalised way to reduce the risk of melanoma recurrence or death. This has not been achieved before in the history of cancer drug development."
Long will present the results at the European Society for Medical Oncology's annual congress in Madrid on the weekend.
The results have been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and will need to go through a process of peer review.
Patients in the trial - conducted across 157 sites worldwide - had not previously received any cancer drug treatment. Of those receiving the combination of intismeran and pembrolizumab, 82% were alive and recurrence-free after two years, compared with 70% of participants treated with pembrolizumab alone.
In a phase III trial, a treatment is tested in a large group of people and compared with standard treatments; it is necessary before drug regulators can approve a medicine for use in the general population.
In recent years, developments in immunotherapy drugs have significantly increased survival rates for people with advanced melanoma.
Dr Jessamy Tiffen, acting deputy director of the Centre for Cancer Innovations at the Centenary Institute, who was not involved in the research, said what was "truly remarkable" about the vaccine was the "deeply personalised nature of the treatment, something cancer researchers have been striving to achieve for decades".
"Where previously oncologists could pick a targeted therapy based on a single gene mutation present in the melanoma, this bespoke mRNA vaccine targets up to 34 gene mutations, unique to each patient. This vaccine, in combination with another type of immunotherapy, then trains the immune system to recognise and eliminate the melanoma, and most importantly, stop it from coming back."
She noted that the treatment, if progressed, would not benefit all people with melanoma. "A significant portion do not respond to the vaccine in the first instance," she said.
"Cancer cells also have an insidious ability to adapt and evade whatever treatment we throw at them. Only time will tell how effective the treatment is beyond two years, but the results are clear that the combination works better than immunotherapy alone, and that's a very exciting development."
The drug manufacturers said it was too early to tell from the data whether the combination treatment improved long-term survival.
Prof Christopher Sweeney, director of the South Australian immunoGENomics Cancer Institute at Adelaide University, described the vaccine as "a step-change approach for how to improve the body's immune system to see cancer cells as foreign and then augment the ability to prevent the cancer cells growing and recurring".
He said more research was needed to see if the approach was effective in patients "who have cancer we can see", or who were not responsive to the immune enhancer pembrolizumab.
The personalised vaccine will not be available as a standard melanoma treatment until it has gone through further study and regulatory review, a process that may take several years.

Image: Five people in dark jackets stand together, smiling outside a stone building marked “Veterinary Clinic.”Some participants in last summer’s SYMCO international wildlife veterinary symposium in South Africa, (left to right) Talia Bendov, V’29; Lottie Mendeno, New Zealand’s School of Veterinary Science – Massey University; Ashley Houck, Iowa State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine; Cabre Capalongo, V’29; and Katie Forrest, the North Carolina State College of Veterinary Medicine. Before the trip, Capalongo had envisioned a career mainly in companion animal medicine. However, after working with lions, rhinos, buffalo, and other wildlife species, she is now considering other possibilities for her future. She’s already thinking about how she can get back. 

“I definitely want to stay involved because this experience opened my eyes to an entirely different side of veterinary medicine,” she said. “Working with such large and diverse species made me realize how much I love working with wildlife.” 

She and her colleagues got lots of hands-on experience with the animals and learned real-life lessons about the importance of conservation. 

“I developed a greater understanding of wildlife medicine and a deeper appreciation for the critical role veterinarians play in conservation,” she said. “I witnessed how caring for individual animals can lead to safeguarding entire populations and ecosystems.” 

Surgeries on big cats, rhino encounters, and making new friends 

Throughout the symposium, the students traveled to wildlife reserves, sanctuaries, and conservation sites across South Africa.

Image: Two people work together to administer an injection to a lion lying on a treatment table.Cabre Capalongo, V’29, vaccinates a lion in South Africa while participating in the SYMCO international wildlife symposium last summer.

They assisted with ovariohysterectomies and vasectomies on lions, giving Capalongo a new perspective on feline surgery. She thought about her own two cats at home. “It was fascinating to be involved in a surgery on such a large feline!”

Oncologie vétérinaire
Tumeur mastocytaire sur la lèvre d'un chien image

L'oncologie vétérinaire est une spécialité de la médecine vétérinaire qui traite du diagnostic et du traitement du cancer chez les animaux. Le cancer est une cause majeure de mortalité chez les animaux de compagnie. Dans une étude, 45 % des chiens ayant atteint l'âge de 10 ans ou plus sont morts d'un cancer.

Les tumeurs cutanées sont le type de tumeur le plus fréquemment diagnostiqué chez les animaux domestiques pour deux raisons : 1. exposition constante de la peau de l'animal au soleil et à l'environnement extérieur, 2. les tumeurs cutanées sont faciles à voir car elles se trouvent à l'extérieur de l'animal.

Veterinary oncology (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterinary_oncology)

Veterinary oncology
Cancer diagnosis and treatment in animals
Mast cell tumor on muzzle of dog

Veterinary oncology is a subspecialty of veterinary medicine that deals with cancer diagnosis and treatment in animals. Cancer is a major cause of death in pet animals. In one study, 45% of the dogs that reached 10 years of age or older died of cancer.

Skin tumors are the most frequently diagnosed type of tumor in domestic animals for two reasons: 1. constant exposure of animal skin to the sun and external environment, 2. skin tumors are easy to see because they are on the outside of the animal.
## History

Specialised veterinary oncology training became available in the 21st century.
## Treatment

The most effective method of treating cancer in animals is surgery. Surgery may involve a marginal excision, where just the capsule is excised; wide excision, where a wider area surrounding the capsule (typically 2–3cm) is excised; or radical excision, where the entire compartment is excised, often taking the form of an amputation.

These statistics, being from the 1960s, may not be an accurate representation of cancer in dogs currently.
## Human-animal cancer connections

Companion animals such as dogs and cats suffer from many of the same types of cancer as humans. Cancer research with dogs has helped in the design of clinical trials for cancer therapy for humans. In the spirit of the One Health movement (global collaborative research on human and animal health) such human-animal connections in cancer research could benefit both humans and animals with cancer in the future.

Animals with cancer also sometimes function as animal sentinels that provide an early warning of carcinogens and an environmental health hazard to humans.
## Ethical issues

Veterinarians use the HHHHHMM Scale to discuss animal quality of life with pet owners before a euthanasia decision is made for a pet with an incurable disease such as cancer (the letters stand for Hurt Hunger Hydration Hygiene Happiness Mobility and "More good days than bad days").

Comparative oncology (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparative_oncology)
【turn1116search23】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 7 months ago; 
Comparative oncology
Comparative oncology integrates the study of oncology in non-human animals into more general studies of cancer biology and therapy. The field encompasses naturally seen cancers in veterinary patients and the extremely low rates of cancers seen in large mammals such as elephants and whales.
## Mammalian cancers

Species that are treated in the veterinary clinic, including dogs, cats, horses and ferrets, present human-relevant cancers.
### Canines

Of these, the dog has the greatest number of incidents. One in four dogs older than 2 dies of cancer, a rate that has increased, which may in part be explained by reductions in other causes of death. Canine cancer shares features with human cancer, including histology, tumor genetics, molecular targets, biological behavior and therapeutic response. Canine histologies include osteosarcoma, melanoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, leukemia, prostate, breast and lung cancer, head and neck cancer, soft tissue sarcomas and bladder cancer. Tumor initiation and progression are influenced by age, nutrition, sex, reproduction and environmental exposure. Canine models support the study of metastasis, disease recurrence and resistance patterns, with relevance to human cancers. Dogs' comparatively accelerated lifespans make them suitable environmental sentinels, as they are exposed to the same environmental carcinogens and develop cancer in a shorter time frame than humans.

Since 2009 some ten drugs have been developed in part based on studies with dogs. On July 3, 2019 FDA approved selinexor (Xpovio) for multiple myeloma patients who have failed five or more therapies. Verdinexor is the veterinary form of this drug. It is under study for canine lymphoma and as a human antiviral therapy.
## Large mammals

Since cancer typically begins as a mutation in a single cell, risks should increase with the number of cells in an organism. Elephants carry 100 times as many cells as humans, while whales have ten times more than elephants.

【turn1116search24】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 10 months ago; 
Soft tissue sarcoma in cats and dogs
Group of malignant tumors in cats and dogs
Soft tissue sarcoma refers to a broad group of tumors that originate from connective tissues. They tend to have similar histologic appearance and biological behavior, and can be either benign or malignant. Soft tissue sarcomas can arise in any part of the pet's body but skin and subcutaneous tumors are the most commonly observed. Soft-tissue sarcomas comprise approximately 15% of all skin and subcutaneous tumors in dogs and approximately 7% of all skin and subcutaneous tumors in cats. The variety of different tumors that fall under the category of soft tissue sarcomas includes fibrosarcoma, hemangiopericytoma, liposarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, malignant fibrous histiocytoma, malignant nerve sheath tumors, myxosarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma, mesenchymoma, and spindle cell tumor.
These tests generally involve blood and serum biochemical tests, chest X-rays to check for metastasis to the lungs and imaging studies [e.g. ultrasound, computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)] to evaluate the extent of the disease.
## Treatment

There are three main treatment options available to treat soft tissue sarcoma in cats and dogs: surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy. Surgery alone or in combination with radiation therapy are used to treat the tumor at its original location, and chemotherapy is usually used to prevent or at least slow down the process of metastasis in pets diagnosed with tumor subtypes known to be highly aggressive.

Skin cancer in cats and dogs
Many types of skin tumors, both benign (noncancerous) and malignant (cancerous), exist in cats and dogs. Approximately 20–40% of primary skin tumors are malignant in dogs and 50–65% are malignant in cats. Not all forms of skin cancer in cats and dogs are caused by sun exposure, but it can happen occasionally. On dogs, the nose and pads of the feet contain sensitive skin and no fur to protect from the sun. Also, cats and dogs with thin or light-colored coats are at a higher risk of sun damage over their entire bodies.
## Diagnosis

Typically, either cytologic or histopathologic analysis of the suspected mass is done prior to initiating treatment. The commonly used diagnostic procedures for skin tumors are fine-needle aspiration cytology and tissue biopsy.

Cytology is an important tool that can help the veterinarian distinguish a tumor from inflammatory lesions. The biopsy technique used will largely depend on the tumor's size and location.

GliomaINK: A Tumor and Anatomy Conditioned Flow Matching Framework for 3D MRI Sequence Synthesis in Glioma Patients (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24044)
【turn1116academia26】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: GliomaINK: A Tumor and Anatomy Conditioned Flow Matching Framework for 3D MRI Sequence Synthesis in Glioma Patients
Authors: Moinak Bhattacharya, Annie Singh, Mohammad Chaudhry, Prateek Prasanna, Gagandeep Singh
Date: Fri Oct 16 15:09:12 2026

Background: Incomplete multiparametric MR examinations limit glioma characterization and downstream AI tools. Generative models can synthesize missing MRI sequences, but anatomical structure and clinically relevant tumor features are challenging to preserve. We propose GliomaINK, an anatomy-guided conditional flow matching framework for cross-sequence 3D brain MRI synthesis. Methods: A 3D SwinUNETR predicted the conditional velocity field while an auxiliary topology-preserving loss encouraged structural consistency. The model was trained on 1,083 patients from the BraTS-AG dataset and independently tested on an in-house clinical cohort. Downstream tasks include image quality, tumor segmentation, IDH1 mutation-status prediction, and overall survival prediction. Two radiologists independently evaluated the anatomical fidelity, pathological representation, and overall image quality of the synthesized images. Results: GliomaINK exhibited the highest PSNR across all six MRI translation directions in both evaluation cohorts. In the BraTS-AG test set, the PSNR reached $25.64\pm0.55$ dB for the T2W-to-T1C synthesis, compared with $13.78\pm0.32$ dB for Pix2Pix and $18.90\pm0.53$ dB for SPADE. For downstream tumor segmentation, the method showed strong performance across tumor subregions with Dice scores reaching $0.928\pm0.014$ for edema, and $0.885\pm0.040$ for enhancing tumor. For the IDH1 mutation-status prediction, GliomaINK achieved the highest AUROC score in four of the six sequence configurations, reaching $0.827\pm0.088$. Conclusion: Anatomy-guided conditional flow matching enables high-fidelity cross-sequence glioma MRI synthesis demonstrating potential for preservation of clinically relevant information in synthesized MRI and improving downstream tasks.

DeDiCa: A Scalable Deconfounding Discrete Causal Generative Model (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23272)
【turn1116academia27】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 6 days ago; 
Title: DeDiCa: A Scalable Deconfounding Discrete Causal Generative Model
Authors: Kunchangtai Liang, Adrián Javaloy, Antonio Vergari, Isabel Valera
Date: Fri Oct 16 10:42:43 2026

We introduce DeDiCa, a practical framework for efficient causal inference with discrete variables and hidden confounding that revisits classical probabilistic modeling through a tensorized parameterization of causal Bayesian networks, enabling tractable inference. Given a causal graph, DeDiCa is trained once on observational data by maximum likelihood, exactly marginalizing over hidden confounders, and can then estimate any (proxy-)identifiable interventional query. Despite this deliberately simple parameterization, DeDiCa matches state-of-the-art neural causal generative models in ATE estimation, while supporting memory-efficient CPU training and exact interventional inference in milliseconds. Compared with causal foundation models, DeDiCa scales more effectively with additional observational samples and achieves competitive accuracy at substantially lower inference time and memory. DeDiCa provides a tractable, accurate, and scalable approach to causal inference in discrete settings with hidden confounding.

PRET is a few-shot system for pan-cancer recognition without example training (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25054)
【turn1116academia28】 [wordlim: 200] Published: 5 days ago; 
Title: PRET is a few-shot system for pan-cancer recognition without example training
Authors: Yi Li, Ziyu Ning, Tianqi Xiang, Qixiang Zhang, Zhihao Lin, Min Yi, Feiyan Feng, Baozhen Zeng, Xuexia Qian, Lu Sun, Jiace Qin, Ling Xiang, Chao Fan, Tian Qin, Qian Wang, Xiu-Wu Bian, Kun-Hsing Yu, Kang Zhang, Qingling Zhang, Xiaomeng Li
Date: Sun Oct 18 06:48:27 2026

Pathological examination stands as the cornerstone in cancer diagnosis, impacting millions worldwide annually. With the shortage of pathologists globally, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged rapidly to automate the diagnostics process. However, conventional AI models require substantial labeled data for each disease, posing huge challenges in scalability and practicality. Therefore, we introduce PRET (pan-cancer recognition without examples training), a few-shot system to achieve flexible, scalable, and effective cancer recognition across diverse organs, hospitals and tasks without training. Evaluated on 23 international benchmarks comprising 4,484 whole-slide images, our method outperforms existing approaches across 20 tasks, achieving over 97% area under the curve on 15 benchmarks with a maximum improvement of 36.76%. Notably, PRET delivers clinical-grade diagnostic performance in lymph node metastasis detection using only eight slide examples, outperforming 11 pathologists. By offering a flexible and cost-effective solution for pan-cancer recognition, PRET paves the way for accessible and equitable AI-based pathology systems, particularly benefiting minority populations and underserved regions.

Title: DR-Learners for Generalizing CATEs from a Randomized Controlled Trial
Authors: Vanessa Rodriguez, Brieuc Lehmann, Karla Diaz-Ordaz
Date: Sun Oct 18 17:03:30 2026

Randomized clinical trials are essential for evaluating interventions, yet average treatment effects can obscure treatment effect heterogeneity, making conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) a natural target. However, restrictive eligibility criteria and differential trial participation can limit the generalizability of these effects to broader target populations. Building on existing DR-Learners, we develop the gDR-Learner for generalizing RCT CATEs to a target population, using cross-fitted machine-learning nuisance estimation. We derive excess-risk bounds in which nuisance errors enter only as products, showing that the estimator achieves oracle-rate convergence despite slower individual nuisance estimation. The variables needed to generalize are rarely measured across the entire target population. We therefore extend the methods to two settings with incomplete covariate information: when certain covariates are measured only in the trial (e.g., biomarkers), and covariates driving trial participation measured only in a subsample of the target population, such as a representative cohort or registry. We construct weighted conformal prediction intervals for individual treatment effects, accounting for covariate shift between the trial and target population. In simulations, the gDR-Learner achieved the lowest estimation error when all covariates were observed relative to standard T- and DR-Learners and an inverse-probability-weighted T-Learner, and also outperformed the latter under incomplete covariate observation. We illustrate the methods by reanalyzing the Coronary Artery Surgery Study, examining treatment effect heterogeneity by prior myocardial infarction and baseline ejection fraction.
